displayQuote: If God did not exist, it would be necessary to invent him

meta.title: Who really said "If God did not exist, it would be necessary to invent him"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuinely Voltaire — a line of verse from his epistle to the author of the Trois imposteurs. And it is an argument against atheists, not against God.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If God did not exist, it would be necessary to invent him'?
meta.ogDescription: Really Voltaire, from a verse epistle of 1768–69. Usually read as cynicism; he wrote it to rebuke the atheists, not the believers.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: It is a line of verse, not a quip in conversation. Voltaire wrote it in his Épître à l’auteur du livre des Trois imposteurs, a poem answering the anonymous atheist tract Traité des trois imposteurs that circulated in French from 1768. The French reads ‘Si Dieu n’existait pas, il faudrait l’inventer’ — and the poem is aimed at d’Holbach’s circle of atheists, not at the devout.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Épître à l’auteur du livre des Trois imposteurs
&Oelig;uvres complètes de Voltaire, ed. Louis Moland, tome 10, pp. 402–405

source.excerpt:
Si les cieux, dépouillés de son empreinte auguste,
Pouvaient cesser jamais de le manifester,
Si Dieu n’existait pas, il faudrait l’inventer.
Que le sage l’annonce, et que les rois le craignent.
trail: The line sits in the sourced section of Wikiquote ↗, credited to the verse epistle rather than to any letter or conversation — it is not among that page’s misattributed or disputed entries.
Wikipedia ↗ has a standalone article on the poem, which exists because of this one line.
The University of Chicago’s Voltaire bibliography ↗ places the poem at tome 10, pp. 402–405 of the Moland &Oelig;uvres complètes (Paris: Garnier, 1877–85), the standard nineteenth-century edition.
The French text of the quatrain is reproduced at French Wikisource ↗ as Épître 104.
source.cutTag: ↑ the famous line is the third of four — the quatrain names God as a restraint on kings, which is the part that gets dropped
source.excerptNote: The English wording in circulation is a plain rendering of the third line and has no single canonical translator; ‘invent him’ and ‘invent Him’ both circulate, and older versions give ‘we should have to invent him.’ All render the same French sentence.

author.name: Voltaire
author.heading: About Voltaire
author.bio: Voltaire — pen name of François-Marie Arouet — was the wit and conscience of the French Enlightenment, author of plays, histories, essays and some fifteen thousand surviving letters. He was a deist, not an atheist, and spent his last decade arguing on two fronts at once: against the Church he mocked for superstition, and against the younger materialists who had decided there was no God at all. This line belongs to the second fight.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: Almost everyone who quotes this line reads it as a wink — religion as a useful fiction, invented to keep the peasants in order. Voltaire meant something closer to the opposite. In 1768 an anonymous atheist tract, the Traité des trois imposteurs, was circulating in French, arguing that Moses, Jesus and Muhammad were three frauds. Voltaire answered it in verse.

His argument is that a universe without a God is not just metaphysically empty but morally unanchored — and the quatrain says so plainly: let the wise proclaim him, and let kings fear him. The line is a rebuke to his fellow philosophes, above all Baron d’Holbach and his atheist circle, not a confession that he was one of them.
context.detailsSummary: A note on the date, and on how the line got its reputation
detailsBody: The poem is dated inconsistently. The University of Chicago’s Voltaire bibliography gives 1768; French Wikisource argues for 1769, noting that Voltaire mentions the piece in a letter of 15 March 1769 and that it appears in collections printed that year; other reference works say 1770, and some older editions filed it under 1771. Nothing turns on the exact year, but no single date is safe to state flatly, so this page gives the range.

The reputation for cynicism is partly Voltaire’s own fault: the line is epigrammatic enough to survive without its quatrain, and once it does, ‘necessary to invent’ reads as an admission of fraud. Read whole, the poem is a deist’s defence of a moral order he thought society could not do without.
context.pull: Read whole, it is a deist arguing with atheists — not an atheist letting something slip.
